title: Should we save to buy in cash, or take a long housing loan?
shortTitle: Cash or loan for a couple
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #325 | SAVE LONGER SO DON'T NEED TO TAKE LOAN
excerpt: A self-employed couple with RM300,000 saved disagree: she wants little or no debt, he wants a normal loan and to invest. Sean suggests a middle ground that suits both.

qa.asker: W, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: W and his girlfriend plan to marry. Both are self-employed, earn about RM7,000 to RM8,000 a month each and have no debts. They have about RM300,000 saved and a budget of RM500,000 to RM600,000 for a first home in KL. She follows Dave Ramsey and wants a big down payment and a 15-year loan, or to save until they can pay cash; he wants a normal loan and to invest the rest.
qa.question: How much should go into the down payment, should they minimise the loan or buy in cash, and is there a balance they can both live with?
qa.quote: My suggestion is to do both and have a medium ground.
qa.answer: Do both. Buy with the market-standard 10% down payment, keep the rest as reserves, and let each partner manage their own money: he takes the loan in his own name and invests, she keeps her savings in safe instruments.

reasons.title: Debt-free advice fits the US, not Malaysia
reasons.body: In the US a 30-year fixed mortgage is about 7.2% and property tax about 1% a year, so short loans make sense there. In Malaysia a good housing loan is about 3.7% to 4% and quit rent and assessment are tiny, so a long loan is cheap money.

reasons.title: Saving for cash can't catch up
reasons.body: A good property rises by around 3% to 5% a year, so savings chase a moving target. And if a property doesn't rise in five years, Sean asks why you would want to buy it at all.

reasons.title: Cash in a house is hard to get back
reasons.body: Put the RM300,000 into the house and you have a home, no savings and a monthly instalment. Selling takes about six to seven months for a freehold unit and longer for leasehold, so in an emergency you would be left with credit cards.

reasons.title: A joint loan wastes a loan slot
reasons.body: A joint 15-year loan costs about the same each month as one person's 35-year loan, and it uses up both people's housing loan slots. Buying in one name keeps the other partner's slots free for later.

actions: Agree how long you could keep your lifestyle if both incomes stopped; Sean keeps about a year of living costs, plus six months of instalments for each property.
For a RM500,000 subsale, budget about 10% down plus 8% for fees, roughly RM90,000, and keep the rest for renovation and reserves.
Buy in one partner's name with a long loan, and keep a shared account only for monthly household bills.
Let the more cautious partner keep their savings in fixed deposits and blue chips, and never borrow from them for investments.
Compare all the buying channels, including bulk purchase, before choosing between new and subsale.
qa.caveat: Sean stresses he is not a certified financial planner and that risk tolerance is personal. The older you are, the more conservative you should be, because there is less time to earn money back.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #325. The quoted answer is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in the episode; loan and deposit rates change. Sean points viewers to the bulk-purchase investment club linked in his video description, which he belongs to.
